This move is getting long in the tooth and I think it's more likely than not that Waller's speech + today's CPI has provided an attractive opportunity to flip from a short to a long risk bias into next week's Anthropic IPO and possibly longer, TBD. This is not an all clear of the structural problems that exist, but a local call that the path to the final destination will not be easy nor in a straight line.

On the robotics and physical AI VC market

Over the last few weeks and months, there’s been a lot of fear in the markets. We believe those concerns are overblown. 

Let me pose a question - were OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Coreweave, etc good investments to make in 2021/2022?

The answer here is pretty clear cut. 

Were there AI companies from that period that weren’t good investments? Sure, but that’s the nature of venture and a small allocation to the top winners could still more than compensate for many poor picks.

Look at this chart. US investments in Robotics has still not even reached pre-ChatGPT levels of investment in AI. At the same time, frontier Physical AI models are already more capable than GPT3.5 at the time ChatGPT came out. 

Roughly half of Anthropic/OpenAIs revenue comes from software development related use. Software development makes up 2-3% of the global labor market. 

Robotics represents physical work which is roughly 50% of the global labor market. 

While I’m very bullish on AI for knowledge work over the next few years, I don’t have a prediction of what happens over the next few weeks and months. Agents have only just started to become really useful for most people and that growth has yet to be realized. 

Could a continued short term market correction in AI spill over into private Physical AI/robotics? Short term maybe some funding rounds for lower quality companies take longer or don’t get done - there are some pools of capital that cross over.

For the companies that otherwise are destined to win, we don’t think there will be much impact. Winners are going to win.

Fluctuations in latent demand for automated physical labor for one shouldn’t change much and if they do, matters little given how little existing penetration and superior economics that robotic solutions provide.

While I don’t have a strong macro view and am definitely not this bearish, the strongest example could be to look at the Great Depression. Tractors were invented before this period but roughly a fifth of the growth in tractor-owning farms between 1920 and 1954 came during the 1930s. 

"The Dust Bowl could blacken the sky, but it could not make the horse cheaper than the tractor."

Companies that face idiosyncratic circumstances will have idiosyncratic results. Technological advances here are accelerating, not slowing and if companies can grow like weeds then we expect funding to follow even if Anthropic raises at $1.3T instead of $2T in its IPO.

Most investors have only started dabbling in this sector and there are mountains of capital looking to get proper exposure. The IPOs of SpaceX and Anthropic are historically large liquidity events that we expect to propel continued downstream VC funding for months and years. 

Let me clear - there will always be a period where the wheat is separated from the chaff. Picking matters. Some capital has gone into winners but also some capital that has gone into losers and we will see the divergence in outcomes over the next few years. 

But with the backdrop of agentic robotic breakthroughs, Multimodel models accelerating R&D for physical AI while also proving a new approach of code as policy, and massively scaled data collection, our optimism for the sector is unwavering

Fluctuations in latent demand for automated physical labor for one shouldn’t change much and if they do, matters little given how little existing penetration and superior economics that robotic solutions provide.

While I don’t have a strong macro view and am definitely not this bearish, the strongest example could be to look at the Great Depression. Tractors were invented before this period but roughly a fifth of the growth in tractor-owning farms between 1920 and 1954 came during the 1930s. 

"The Dust Bowl could blacken the sky, but it could not make the horse cheaper than the tractor."

Companies that face idiosyncratic circumstances will have idiosyncratic results. Technological advances here are accelerating, not slowing and if companies can grow like weeds then we expect funding to follow even if Anthropic raises at $1.3T instead of $2T in its IPO.

Most investors have only started dabbling in this sector and there are mountains of capital looking to get proper exposure. The IPOs of SpaceX and Anthropic are historically large liquidity events that we expect to propel continued downstream VC funding for months and years. 

Let me clear - there will always be a period where the wheat is separated from the chaff. Picking matters. Some capital has gone into winners but also some capital that has gone into losers and we will see the divergence in outcomes over the next few years. 

But with the backdrop of agentic robotic breakthroughs, Multimodel models accelerating R&D for physical AI while also proving a new approach of code as policy, and massively scaled data collection, our optimism for the sector is unwavering

I wouldn't characterize the state of enterprise AI adoption this way. Broadly, I would say there are two variables in measuring the ROI of AI in an organization: 
1. The task you are automating or augmenting 
2. Does this business have any fucking idea why they are successful? 

#1 The task. 
Let's take a very simple example. Closing out a support ticket from a customer. Most companies know how much this costs by channel - say, $40 to pick up the phone, $15 to answer it by email, $5 by chat. This is calculating using things like the agent salaries, the headcount that supports them, the technology they use, the facilities, and any travel and training expenses

Now imagine you can use AI to *successfully* answer a question and the AI company you use charges you 70 cents for that. OK, you really clearly know the ROI of AI in this specific, bounded, use case.

Consider other tasks. The velocity with which you ship new products. A bit fuzzier but not a crazy task to determine whether 1) Developer productivity has increased 2) Whether that is bending the slope of your revenue curve upward.

Farther out on the curve. Being able to now generate 21 different versions of a marketing campaign's creative using your brand design assets. Making 40% of analytics requests self-service instead of being stuck in a queue for humans to answer. Quite a bit messier to measure direct ROI.

#2 Does the company have it's shit together? 

Do they know what is actually driving the business forward? I think that the answer for many businesses is actually, No. Do they reliably know who their top performers are? Do they know the actual 2-3 inputs that drive revenue growth? Not only do they know them but can they accelerate them? If you asked 10 people at the company what "the most important thing" was for the business, would they give the same answer? Again, I think the answer is mostly No. 

If you do not deeply understand your business, what is driving it, and who is driving it, it is quite hard to know whether AI is helping you. 
----------
TL;DR. For some tasks it is quite easy to measure the ROI. For others, less so. For some businesses who have their shit together, it is quite easy to measure the ROI. For others, less so.

$WGS earnings. Market cap roughly $1.6B. The good: revenue $123M, margins improved to 72%, adjusted profit $8.6M, reimbursements up 5%, genome collection rates improving, and Medicaid coverage expanding. The bad: volume growth slowing, guidance lowered, reimbursement documentation creating delays, and Medicare reimbursement cuts presenting a 2027 headwind. What needs to happen for the stock to recover? The company needs to reaccelerate volume growth, improve reimbursement collection, reduce payment delays, and demonstrate that expanding Medicaid coverage can translate into sustainable revenue and earnings growth. The entire genomics sector has been under pressure, with even $ILMN down roughly 30%. I believe $WGS will start running again when the sector recovers. I’m not increasing my exposure today because I already have enough, but I’m not selling either. If I had less exposure, I would probably be buying more. 

When $WGS reached $100, it got there without any logic. 
There was no meaningful improvement in the underlying business, yet the stock price had doubled. Now it’s being oversold again because of market sentiment and pressure across the entire sector. This is simply the nature of stock market cycles. Prices can become completely disconnected from business fundamentals in both directions. You buy when pessimism becomes excessive and sell when optimism exceeds logic.

Nobody voted for it and it doesnt appear anywhere you can see it. But its a tax all the same, and once you see it, the rest starts to make sense... why the system feels rigged, why your parents path to wealth stopped working, and why the Exponential Age is the only way out.
